why: The RL change is a global low-rank format/deliberation shift, not an error detector, so its difference peaks rarely sit at the first wrong step.
A near-linear shift along a few directions with a wide accuracy plateau gives about 40 % of the 410-to-463 gap at a quarter dose.
At half dose the low-rank format/length readout is mostly switched, so about 70 % of the cued gap is recovered.
At three-quarter dose the shift is nearly complete, so the score is within a few points of RL.
The RL change is only ~0.24 % of weight norm, so at a = 1.5 the model is still in the linear regime and stays near RL instead of collapsing to the token cap as in the code-RL and Bolmo dose curves.
In the linear regime at a = 1.5 the model keeps its features, so almost no answers degrade into word salad.
Without the cue the quarter-dose shift recovers about a third of the 224-to-463 plain-prompt gap.
At half dose the low-rank readout is mostly switched, about 70 % of the plain-prompt gap, matching the plateau that DARE's noise tolerance implies.
The length readout moves linearly with the dose, so mean tokens move a quarter of the way from the cued base (~3,930) toward RL (~4,690).
A random matched-norm difference is high-rank noise with no component along the functional directions, so it leaves the cued base at 410.
The random difference acts like a reseed, so it fixes only the share of the base's 90 wrong problems that a fresh base sample would fix.
Half dose gives about 446 right with ~14 resampling losses, so it fixes about 50 of the base's 90 wrong problems.
High-rank noise does not move the format/length readout, so mean tokens stay at the cued base's ~3,930.
The functional change is a coherent low-dimensional shift in the residual stream, so one mean vector per layer captures a large part of it on cued-base text.
On RL's own text the deliberation directions are engaged more uniformly, so the mean vector closes more KL than on base text, as every arm does (69 vs 86 % for all MLP).
The MLP carries about two thirds of the shift, so an MLP-only mean vector closes about two thirds of the all-layer constant arm on base text.
Same two-thirds share of the constant arm, on RL text.
The low-rank shift is dense across neurons, so 0.13 % of neurons, even always-on ones, carry only about their proportional share of it.
Same dense-support argument, on RL text, where every arm closes somewhat more.
